article.h1: Fitzpatrick Skin Type Test: A Simple Self-Quiz and What the Result Means
article.body_html:
A Fitzpatrick skin type test sorts people into one of six types (I to VI) based on how their skin usually reacts to sun: whether it burns, whether it tans, and how much. Below is a short informal self-quiz built on that idea, plain-language descriptions of each type, and a clear explanation of why the result is not your skin tone, undertone or foundation shade.

What the Fitzpatrick scale is (and what it isn't)

A six-type scale based on how skin reacts to sun

The Fitzpatrick scale was developed in the 1970s by dermatologist Thomas Fitzpatrick. It describes a person's typical reaction to sun exposure, from skin that burns easily and barely tans (Type I) to skin that very rarely burns and has deep natural pigmentation (Type VI). It is a rough sorting tool, not a precise measurement.

Why it isn't a skin tone, undertone or makeup shade chart

The scale describes sun reaction, not how your skin looks. It says nothing about whether your undertone is warm, cool or neutral, and it does not tell you which foundation, blush or clothing colors suit you. Two people can share a type and look quite different.

A note up front: educational and cosmetic only

This article is a general, educational guide with a cosmetic focus. The quiz is an informal self-check for curiosity and for understanding the difference between sun reaction, tone and undertone. It is not a clinical tool.

Before you take the test: how to answer fairly

Think about your natural baseline, not your current tan

Answer for your skin's usual pattern, not how it looks right now. A current tan, or one unusual sunburn after a very long day outside, can skew the result.

Recall past reactions; don't test yourself in the sun

Base your answers on what has happened before, such as the first long day outdoors at the start of a sunny season without sunscreen. Please do not expose your skin to the sun on purpose to find out. If you have always used sun protection and can't remember, say so honestly and treat the result as very uncertain.

Answer from experience rather than guessing

If you're unsure, ask someone who has seen you after a day outside. Your memory of how pink or sore you got is a better guide than an assumption based on your skin color.

A simple Fitzpatrick skin type self-test

This is a simplified, informal self-check written for this guide. It has no points to add up. Each answer points to a type, and you compare the two results. Longer questionnaires also ask about other traits, for example:

  • Eye color: from light blue, gray or green through to dark brown.
  • Natural hair color: from red or light blond through to black.
  • Freckling: from many freckles to none.

This quiz leaves those out and uses only burning and tanning, the core of the scale. If you want the fuller version, a dermatologist or doctor can take you through it.

Question 1: How does your skin usually react to a first long stretch of unprotected midday sun?

  • A. Burns every time, often painfully, and peels: points to Type I
  • B. Burns easily and usually peels: points to Type II
  • C. Sometimes burns mildly: points to Type III
  • D. Rarely burns: points to Type IV
  • E. Very rarely or almost never burns: points to Type V or VI

Option E covers both V and VI on purpose, so Question 2 does the work of telling them apart.

Question 2: What does your skin do afterward in terms of tanning?

  • A. Doesn't tan; turns red or freckles: points to Type I
  • B. Tans lightly and slowly, if at all: points to Type II
  • C. Tans gradually to a light or moderate brown: points to Type III
  • D. Tans fairly easily to a moderate brown: points to Type IV
  • E. Tans very easily and deeply: points to Type V
  • F. Has deep natural pigmentation, and any change from sun is hard to see: points to Type VI

How to read your answers

  • Both answers point to the same type: that is your best-fit type.
  • They point to neighboring types (for example III and IV): note both, such as "III to IV".
  • They are far apart (for example I and IV): your memory may be unreliable, or your reaction may be unusual. Consider the quiz inconclusive.

Whatever you land on, it is a rough guess based on memory.

The six Fitzpatrick types in plain language

Types I and II: burn easily, tan little or not at all

Type I typically burns almost every time and does not tan. Type II burns easily and may tan a little. Both are usually associated with lighter natural skin, though skin color alone does not decide the type.

Types III and IV: burn sometimes or rarely, tan gradually to easily

Type III sometimes burns and tans gradually to a light or moderate brown. Type IV burns rarely and tans fairly easily. These types cover a wide range of looks, including light-olive and medium-brown skin.

Types V and VI: rarely or almost never burn, deeper natural pigmentation

Type V rarely burns and tans readily. Type VI very rarely burns and has the deepest natural pigmentation. Rarely burning does not mean never, and it does not mean sun protection is optional.

What to do if you fall between two types

This is common. Because the scale is a rough grouping, many people sit on a border. Note both types and move on to the cosmetic steps below, which matter more for color and makeup anyway.

Fitzpatrick type vs skin tone vs undertone

A quick comparison: what each measures and what it's used for

TermWhat it describesTypically used for
Fitzpatrick typeHow skin reacts to sun (burning and tanning)A rough, self-reported sun-reaction grouping
Skin tone (depth)How light or deep your skin looksFoundation depth, concealer, bronzer
UndertoneThe warm, cool or neutral hue beneath the surfaceFoundation match, blush, jewelry metals, clothing colors

Why two people with the same type can look quite different

One Type III person may have a golden, warm undertone and another a cool, pink one. Their sun reactions are similar, but a peachy blush and gold jewelry might flatter the first, while a rosy blush and silver might suit the second.

Where to go to find your depth and undertone instead

For color and makeup decisions, use our guides to finding your skin tone depth and undertone and simple undertone tests.

What your result can and can't tell you

It's a rough, self-reported sorting tool

Your answers depend on memory, past sun habits, climate and whether you used sunscreen. That makes the result approximate.

Its limits, including for darker skin tones

The scale groups a very wide range of skin into a few types, and it is often criticized for not capturing the variation within deeper skin tones. Types V and VI in particular cover a lot of ground, so the number is not a full description of anyone.

Every type needs sun protection

A higher number does not mean you are safe in the sun. Widely accepted basics such as sunscreen, shade and protective clothing apply to every type. A quiz result should never replace advice from a dermatologist or doctor.

What to use for makeup and color choices instead

Depth and undertone for foundation, concealer and blush

Match foundation to your depth first, then fine-tune for undertone. Warm undertones often suit terracotta or peach blush, cool undertones often suit rose or berry, and neutral undertones can wear both.

Vein, jewelry and white-vs-cream tests as starting points

Greenish veins, gold jewelry that looks natural on you, and cream looking better than stark white tend to suggest warm. Blue or purple veins, silver jewelry and crisp white tend to suggest cool. These are hints, not proof, so check them against several tests.

Using natural-light photos to compare shades

Stand facing a window, hold the camera at eye level and skip filters. Compare shades against your jaw and neck, not just your cheek. For more on previewing looks, see our makeup virtual try-on guide.

Where FitCheck AI can fit in

FitCheck AI does not determine your Fitzpatrick type. It can help with the cosmetic follow-up. The live skin analysis with the camera gives an AI skin overview with cosmetic beauty suggestions, which you can read alongside your own depth and undertone notes.

The app also has an AI makeup assistant that gives personalized makeup suggestions and feedback based on your appearance, and a live virtual makeup try-on that previews looks such as lipstick on your own face. For makeup and skin, face natural light, hold the camera at eye level and avoid filters. For outfits, the style breakdown includes color match feedback you can use as a second opinion. All of it is a starting point, not an objective or professional assessment. The AI feedback is not medical advice, so please see a dermatologist or doctor for any skin concern.

faqs.question: Can I take a Fitzpatrick test from a photo?
faqs.answer: Not reliably. The scale is based on how your skin reacts to sun over time, which a photo can't show, and lighting and filters change how skin looks. A photo can help with cosmetic choices like shade and undertone, but not with your sun-reaction type.

faqs.question: Is the Fitzpatrick scale the same as my skin tone?
faqs.answer: No. The scale describes burning and tanning, while skin tone describes how light or deep your skin looks, and undertone is the warm, cool or neutral hue beneath. Use depth and undertone for makeup and clothing colors.

faqs.question: Does a higher type number mean I'm safe in the sun?
faqs.answer: No. Higher types tend to burn less often, but sunscreen, shade and protective clothing are widely recommended for every type.

faqs.question: Can the result change over time?
faqs.answer: The type is meant to describe your typical natural reaction, so it shouldn't swing with a seasonal tan. Your answers may shift if you remember your past reactions more clearly, which is why the quiz is only a rough guide.

faqs.question: Should I ask a dermatologist for my type?
faqs.answer: If you want a more thorough answer than an informal quiz, a dermatologist or doctor can take you through a proper questionnaire and discuss any questions you have.

review.notes: The article fits the informational intent. It gives a usable two-question quiz, plain-language descriptions of types I to VI, and a clear explanation of how the scale differs from skin tone and undertone. Safety framing is good: it tells readers not to sun-test, says every type needs sun protection, and says the quiz is informal and not clinical. The Fitzpatrick history and type descriptions are accurate in broad terms, and the app section stays within APP_FACTS. It states that the app does not determine Fitzpatrick type, makes no accuracy claims, and carries the 'not medical advice' disclaimer. Minor, non-blocking suggestions: (1) The Q1 wording 'Rarely burns' for IV and 'Very rarely' for V/VI is slightly inconsistent with the later description 'Type V rarely burns'. Aligning the wording would help. (2) The quiz drops the eye color, hair color and freckling questions of the standard questionnaire, but the article discloses this. (3) Confirm the internal links (/blog/what-is-my-skin-tone/, /blog/what-color-undertones-do-i-have/, /blog/makeup-virtual-try-on-guide/, /ai-skin-analysis/) resolve before publishing. (4) The FitCheck section is a short, relevant add-on and does not feel like a hard sell.
